title.source: How can we tell a shared history fairly?

essentialQuestion.source: How can a small exhibition connect sources from different places without claiming more than the evidence shows?

learningGoal.source: Plan a small exhibit panel that credits two sources, makes one connection they support, and names one limit and one missing perspective.

warmUp.question.source: Imagine a label next to an old object. What would help you trust it?

warmUp.options.0.source: It says where the object is from

warmUp.options.2.source: It names who made or kept it

evidence.question.source: Pick two cards from different places. What can each one show, and what can it not show?

evidence.cards.0.sources.0.caption.source: Card A: Butuan, the Philippines. Old boat planks, photographed in 2015 (Lesson 2)

evidence.cards.0.sources.0.details.0.source: A photographer called Lee took this photo of planks from an old Butuan boat on display at the Balangay Shrine Museum in Butuan.

evidence.cards.0.sources.0.details.1.source: It shows: surviving planks of a boat, kept and shown today.

evidence.cards.0.sources.0.details.2.source: It cannot show: where the boat sailed, or who was on board.

evidence.cards.0.sources.0.details.3.source: Credit: Lee, 2015, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

evidence.cards.0.sources.1.caption.source: Card B: Melaka, Malaysia. A map made in 1604 (Lesson 3)

evidence.cards.0.sources.1.details.0.source: Manuel Godinho de Herédia drew this map of the city of Melaka and the land around it in 1604, when Portugal ruled the port.

evidence.cards.0.sources.1.details.1.source: It shows: what this mapmaker chose to draw of the port in his own time.

evidence.cards.0.sources.1.details.2.source: It cannot show: the Melaka of the 1400s, or how each person living there saw the city.

evidence.cards.0.sources.1.details.3.source: Credit: Manuel Godinho de Herédia, 1604, Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

evidence.cards.0.sources.2.caption.source: Card C: Banda, Indonesia. A Dutch painting made about 1662–1663 (Lesson 4)

evidence.cards.0.sources.2.details.0.source: A painting of the island of Banda Neira with the buildings of the Dutch East India Company, the VOC, and a Dutch ship. It is credited to Johannes Vingboons and kept by the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.

evidence.cards.0.sources.2.details.1.source: It shows: ships and buildings, as a Dutch artist pictured them about 40 years after 1621.

evidence.cards.0.sources.2.details.2.source: It cannot show: what the people of Banda went through in 1621, told in their own words.

evidence.cards.0.sources.2.details.3.source: Credit: Johannes Vingboons, about 1662–1663, Rijksmuseum, public domain.

evidence.cards.0.sources.3.caption.source: Card D: Timor-Leste. A school, photographed in 2024 (Lesson 9)

evidence.cards.0.sources.3.details.0.source: A photographer called Ponsyano took this photo of a school building in Timor-Leste on 21 November 2024.

evidence.cards.0.sources.3.details.1.source: It shows: one school building today.

evidence.cards.0.sources.3.details.2.source: It cannot show: whether every child can go to school, or how schools were rebuilt after 1999.

evidence.cards.0.sources.4.caption.source: Card E: Hội An, Viet Nam. A covered bridge, photographed in 2018 (Lesson 10)

evidence.cards.0.sources.4.details.0.source: A photographer called Christophe95 took this photo of the covered bridge in Hội An on 27 July 2018.

evidence.cards.0.sources.4.details.1.source: It shows: a place from the old trading port that survives today.

evidence.cards.0.sources.4.details.2.source: It cannot show: the traders and residents of the 1400s to the 1800s.

evidence.cards.0.sources.4.details.3.source: Credit: Christophe95, 2018, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

evidence.cards.0.sources.5.caption.source: Card F: Borobudur, Indonesia. Conservation work, photographed in 1976 (Lesson 11)

evidence.cards.0.sources.5.details.0.source: Gerard Bolla took this black-and-white photo of the restoration of Borobudur for UNESCO in 1976.

evidence.cards.0.sources.5.details.1.source: It shows: a moment of modern repair work, with scaffolding on the monument.

evidence.cards.0.sources.5.details.2.source: It cannot show: what the builders of the 700s and 800s planned or thought.

evidence.cards.0.sources.5.details.3.source: Credit: UNESCO / Gerard Bolla, 1976, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO.

read.sections.0.text.source: A museum or classroom exhibition is made from choices. A curator decides which sources to show, how to date and credit them, and which questions to ask. A good label lets a visitor tell what is seen from what is guessed. No single object, map or photo can tell the whole history of a region. The National Museum of Cambodia, in Phnom Penh, is one example. It says its work is to show, protect and explain Cambodia's cultural treasures. It holds sculptures, pottery and other objects. That is how one museum explains its own collection. It does not speak for every community in Southeast Asia.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: An exhibition is made from choices. A curator picks the sources to show. The curator gives each one a date and a credit. A good label shows what we see and what we guess. One object cannot tell the story of a whole region. The National Museum of Cambodia is one example. It says it shows, protects and explains Cambodia's treasures. That is the story of one museum. It does not speak for everyone.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Compare what two sources can show

read.sections.1.text.source: The second picture is a photo of the National Museum of Cambodia, taken on 2 March 2011 by a photographer who uses the name Dtfman. You can see red buildings with tall roofs around a garden. You cannot see the objects inside, or how the displays were chosen. The museum's own description gives a different kind of information. It says the buildings went up between 1917 and 1924, and the museum opened in 1920. It also says what the museum aims to do. So one source helps with what the place looks like. The other helps with what the museum says it does. Both sources have limits.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: The second picture is a photo of the museum from 2011. You can see red buildings and a garden. You cannot see the objects inside. The museum also wrote about itself. It says it opened in 1920. It says what it wants to do. So the photo shows what the place looks like. The writing tells us what the museum does. Each source has limits.

read.sections.2.text.source: UNESCO's Shared Histories lessons, made with teachers and historians from Southeast Asia, help learners look for links between people and places across the region. Now you can be the curator. Choose two source cards from different places or different parts of this course. Explain a careful connection: something both sources help us ask about. Do not invent a meeting or a journey that the sources do not show. Then say what is still uncertain, and whose perspective is missing. Put a credit under each source so someone else can check it. You can make your panel on paper or out loud. A fair account can say, "This source does not tell us."

read.sections.2.simpler.source: UNESCO made Shared Histories lessons with teachers from Southeast Asia. They help learners find links between places. Now you are the curator. Choose two cards from different places. Say one thing both sources help us ask about. Do not invent a trip. Say what we still do not know. Say whose perspective is missing. Put a credit under each source, so others can check it. It is fair to say, "This source does not tell us."

read.glossary.0.definition.source: A person who chooses objects for a display and explains them.

read.glossary.0.example.source: A curator decides which two sources go on the panel.

read.glossary.1.definition.source: Something from the past or present that we can study as evidence.

read.glossary.1.example.source: The 1604 map of Melaka is a source about the port.

read.glossary.2.definition.source: How a person sees things, shaped by where they are and why.

read.glossary.2.example.source: A trader's perspective on a port may differ from a mapmaker's.

read.glossary.3.definition.source: A note that names who made a source and where it is kept.

read.glossary.3.example.source: The credit under the bridge photo names Christophe95 and the year 2018.

read.checks.0.question.source: Can a photo of a museum's outside show all that is inside?

read.checks.0.options.0.text.source: No, it shows the outside only

read.checks.0.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. You can see buildings and a garden. The objects and the choices about displays are inside.

read.checks.0.options.1.text.source: Yes, if the photo is very clear

read.checks.0.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. Even a clear photo of the outside cannot show what is inside. Look at the second part of the reading.

read.checks.0.options.2.text.source: Yes, because it is a real photo

read.checks.0.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. A real photo still has limits. Think about what the camera could not see.

read.checks.1.question.source: Why do you put a credit under each source in your exhibit?

read.checks.1.options.0.text.source: To make the panel look longer

read.checks.1.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. A credit has a job to do. Look at the end of the third part of the reading.

read.checks.1.options.1.text.source: So others can find and check it

read.checks.1.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. A credit names who made the source and where it is kept, so others can check it.

read.checks.1.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. Your ideas go in your panel. The credit is about the source itself.

read.checks.2.question.source: Which two cards could you put side by side? What could they help you ask?

read.checks.2.placeholder.source: For example: Card ... and Card ... both help us ask about ...

write.prompt.source: Pick two cards from different places or lessons, and plan a panel. Give each card a credit. Then write one link both sources support, one limit and one missing perspective.

write.sentenceStarters.0.source: My first source is ..., made in ... by ...

write.sentenceStarters.1.source: My second source is ..., made in ... by ...

write.sentenceStarters.2.source: Both sources help us ask about ...

write.sentenceStarters.4.source: A perspective that is missing is ...

write.planningBoxes.0.source: My two sources and their credits

write.selfCheck.0.source: I chose two sources from different places or lessons, with a credit for each.

write.selfCheck.1.source: I made one connection that both sources support.

write.selfCheck.2.source: I named one limit and one missing perspective.

write.example.source: My first source is a photo of old boat planks from Butuan, in the Philippines, taken by Lee in 2015. My second source is a map of Melaka, made in 1604 by Manuel Godinho de Herédia. Both sources help us ask how people built boats and used ports by the sea. One limit is that they come from different places and times. They do not prove that this boat ever went to Melaka. A perspective that is missing is a sailor's own account.

speak.partnerTask.source: Present your panel to a partner in about one minute. Your partner asks, "What supports this part?" and gives you one suggestion.

speak.independentTask.source: Read your panel aloud to yourself. Then write an answer to the question, "What supports this part?"

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Some cards touch hard history: Banda in 1621 (the VOC took control by force), Timor-Leste after 1999, and colonial rule in Melaka. Keep panels about what each source can and cannot show, and never ask learners to connect a source to their own or their family's experiences of war, displacement, home country, religion or ethnicity. If learners look up the National Museum on the Ministry of Culture's page, preview it first: its "History of the Museum" part currently holds an unrelated passage about the S-21 prison, which is not for this lesson.

educatorNotes.0.source: Aim: learners plan a short, fair, credited exhibit panel from two sources in different places or lessons. Evidence move: model a connection between two cards without inventing a direct voyage (for example Butuan planks and the 1604 Melaka map help us ask about boats and ports, but neither proves the boat went to Melaka). Rubric, four equal parts: accurate dates and places; two properly credited sources; a connection the evidence supports; a limit or missing perspective. Give concrete feedback, not a score alone. A panel can be written, drawn on paper or spoken; the brief's 80 to 120 words is a guide, and the example is shorter.

educatorNotes.1.source: Misconception to address: that any two sources from the region prove direct contact between their places. Source caveats: the card details repeat what Lessons 2, 3, 4, 9, 10 and 11 say; check them against those lessons' final versions. The museum's aims and dates (buildings 1917 to 1924, opened 1920) come from Cambodia's Ministry of Culture and Fine Arts. The photo shows the courtyard and a few old cannons on display, not any object from inside. The National Museum is one institution's example, not the voice of every Cambodian or Southeast Asian community.
